Is it one bot or all of them?

All of them. My bots share one computer, so when it hangs, every bot that needs it (shell, browser, desktop, scheduled routines) fails together. Plain chat and connectors still work, so the bots answer but can't do any real work on the machine.

What's happening:

Since about Nov 12, shell commands time out after roughly 14 minutes, and desktop screenshots and browser tasks hang or get cut off partway. Scheduled routines that need the computer have been failing most days. At one point the load average was over 200 with under 1 GB of memory free. Clearing old helper processes and deleting unused bots brought it down to about 1 for a while, but the timeouts came back. Deleting bots also didn't shut down their desktops, so about 17 desktops and their browsers kept running and holding roughly 6 GB.

Have I tried restarting?

Yes. Update Bot's Computer won't complete, and Reset fails with an error saying the computer may be half-reset. Quitting and reopening the app and hitting Retry Reset didn't clear it either.

Ticket: T-K23131.

Support asked me not to reset or update the computer while they look into it, so I've left it alone since.

It feels like software engineering got replaced with... 20% management and 80% code review this year.

If you think engineering is just implementation, this is accurate. But that's not all there is to engineering! There's so much on the systems design side, the factory engineering, that's worth solving now:

- Planning: When should the agent involve humans to draft a plan or proceed with implementation? What questions should it ask? What goes into a good product or technical spec?

- Implementation: Now that agents are writing code, how do we optimize the cost and quality of that code? What access permissions do agents have across secrets, MCPs, and skills?

- Review: How do we give agents the tools to verify their own work end-to-end before tagging us for review? How can agents assess the risk of a PR and include that assessment in the pull request to save humans time?

These are some of the most important problems for engineers to solve this next year.

Elon Musk says xAI might now have “the best training stack software in the world” after rewriting everything from scratch over six to eight months

“And this meant rewriting the entire training, RL and inference stack from scratch, versus using JAX and SGLang, which is sort of kind of freeware from Google, more or less, but not as good as what they’ve got internally by far. “So we’ve been rewriting the entire training stack. When I say the entire training stack, I mean everything. posts.text:
A lot of people have real trouble thinking about the aggregate behavior of groups. They can only think about individuals.

So they think about Elon Musk as an individual. Maybe they think that he must be retarded, because they need that for emotional reasons. Or maybe they think he is a talented rocket designer.

But even if they realize he understands rockets, they can only think about him as an individual doing tasks. Not about his impact on what the whole company does.

If Elon Musk is just a talented rocket designer, then he can spend all day, every day, improving rocket designs.

But he is just one of 7000 engineers. So even if did a perfect job, he would only improve progress by about .014%

So, when a midwit looks at SpaceX, he sees 7000 engineers, and says to himself "Elon Musk cannot possibly be designing the whole damn rocket himself. These people are giving him too much credit."

This would be absolutely true if Musk were just a some random SpaceX engineer. But he isn't. He's the absolute dictator of the whole damn company.

He decides, with absolute and unquestionable authority, which behaviors are punished and which are rewarded.

Why is this important?

When I worked at Boeing, on various classified projects, I naively came in with the assumption that I was a software engineer, employed to design and build functional software as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Because of this, I focused on functionality and efficiency, for example suggesting changes that would obviate the need for entire projects and software components.

And I very rapidly became persona non grata.

At first, this caused me to adopt an air of aggrieved innocence. I was just trying to do my job well, and I was being punished for it.

Then I gradually came to realize that I hadn't properly understood what my job was, or what the actual mission of Boeing Defense, Space, and Security was.

Boeing DSS was not an aerospace company. Boeing DSS was a fraud company.

Its goal was twofold. First, to maximize transfer of public tax dollars to stockholder pockets. Second, to maintain the appearance of being an aerospace company, to prevent the fraud from being exposed.

Which meant that my real job was twofold. First, to generate billable hours. Second, to look busy.

This is why Space Launch System sucks. Why it is always late when it doesn't fail outright. Why it is at 300% of its target budget. Why it leaves American astronauts stranded and needing a lift from SpaceX.

That's because, for Boeing, building rockets is a side quest. Something they have to do to look busy. Yes, a rocket does occasionally fly, but that's just happening so programs don't get shut down.

For Boeing, coming in early and under budget would actually be failure. The system is functioning exactly as designed.

The cost, not the rocket, is the goal.

Musk and SpaceX don't work like that.

Unlike Boeing executives, Musk is not a useless grifter asshole. He is an entirely different kind of asshole... a rocket obsessed sperg.

So, at SpaceX, engineers do not get rewarded for generating billable hours. They get rewarded for making rockets fly. And for all the subtasks of this, like figuring out how to make rockets lighter, figuring out how to make engines reignite better, figuring out how to make rocket exhaust not destroy launch pads, etc.

And this attracts engineers who care about rockets. You've seen them on broadcasts, crying on open microphones because they dedicated their lives to something and it just flew.

As a rocket engineer, who designs rockets, Musk is probably replaceable. As a rocket company engineer, who designs rocket companies, he is not.

For over 50 years, the US space industry stagnated precisely for the lack of a Musk-like figure, who could not only create an effective aerospace company, but who could thereby demonstrate what an effective aerospace company looks like.

Which makes it much more difficult for fraudsters to get away with fraud.

I'm envious. I wish I could have worked for an aerospace company instead of a fraud company.

But what's more important is that some of us now no longer have to play "who gets the most cheese?".

They get to play "What can we build today?".

If exponential change will continue its pace, I can't imagine the rate we'll engage with in 10 years. Disease found in the morning, cure found by dinner. Problem surfaces on a Tuesday, a better solution is found on a Wednesday.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at http://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics.
